869.title: Keeping it abroad (Daniel 1)
869.hook: young exiles keep their food laws at the king's court
869.howItsDone: Jews who keep kosher find ways to keep it while traveling, at work and at other people's tables, and the story of Daniel and his friends is told as an example of keeping Jewish practice far from home.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Esther went in to the king uncalled, and named the enemy at her own table. Your line was if I perish, I perish. Who did you speak up for? Today, a new book, and another royal court. Day eight hundred sixty-nine.

A plate arrives from the king's own table. In Babylon, King Nebuchadnezzar has ordered some of the young captives from Judah to be trained for his court: good-looking, quick, skilled in learning. They'll be taught the learning and the tongue of the Chaldeans. They'll eat the king's food and drink the king's wine. Among them are four young men: Daniel, Hananiah, Mishael and Azariah. And the first thing the court does is rename them. Daniel becomes Belteshazzar. Hananiah becomes Shadrach, Mishael becomes Meshach, Azariah becomes Abed-nego. New names, a new language, new books. They accept all of it. Then the plate comes, and Daniel draws a line.
screen: `CAPTIVES TRAINED FOR THE KING.` → `FOUR NEW NAMES.` → `THEN THE KING'S PLATE.`

segments.voice: In the King James words: "But Daniel purposed in his heart that he would not defile himself with the portion of the king's meat, nor with the wine which he drank." Purposed in his heart. The decision is made inside before it's said out loud. The text doesn't spell out why the king's food would defile him. Some readers point to the food laws of the Torah. Some say the food and wine had been offered to idols. Some hear something simpler: a captive who won't depend on the king's table for everything. What the text does show is how he does it. He doesn't make a scene. He asks the official in charge, who is afraid: if these young men look worse than the others, the king will have his head. So Daniel offers a test. "Prove thy servants, I beseech thee, ten days; and let them give us pulse to eat, and water to drink." Pulse means plain food from seeds: vegetables, beans. Ten days later, the text says, they look healthier than all the young men who ate the king's portion. And God, it adds, gave the four of them knowledge and skill in all learning and wisdom. So they study Babylon's books, answer to Babylon's names, serve Babylon's king, and still keep one thing that marks who they are. That's the shape of this story: live fully where you are, and keep something the place can't take away.
screen: `NEW NAMES, NEW LANGUAGE, NEW FOOD.` · then, large: `DANIEL PURPOSED IN HIS HEART.` · `A POLITE TEN-DAY TEST.` · `PULSE AND WATER.` · then: `LIVE THERE. KEEP ONE THING.`

segments.voice: Today's practice is to keep one practice in a strange place. Sit, and let your shoulders drop. Choose one small thing you do that marks who you are. A blessing before you eat. A minute of quiet. A candle. A word of thanks before sleep. Now find the place where it's hardest to keep: a work trip, a friend's house, a loud lunchroom, a hospital, a day when you're simply tired. See yourself there. See yourself doing your small thing anyway, quietly, without a speech. If you pray, you can ask in words from your tradition for help keeping it. The bell holds the time.
Pulse. The plain food of vegetables and beans Daniel asked for instead of the king's meat and wine. Today's word.
Your line: keep it abroad. Today, do your small thing in the place where it's least convenient, and do it politely. Day eight hundred sixty-nine.

refuse loudly in front of the court.

what it means: young captives accept new names and new learning, but keep one line: they won't defile themselves with the king's food.
what a scholar hears: the text never says exactly why. readers point to the food laws, to food offered to idols, or to not depending on the king's table.

870.title: A fourth in the fire (Daniel 3)
870.hook: three young men refuse to bow and walk unharmed in the furnace
870.howItsDone: Jewish teachers tell the story of Hananiah, Mishael and Azariah, the Hebrew names of Shadrach, Meshach and Abed-nego, as an example of refusing to worship an idol even at great risk.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Daniel purposed in his heart and asked for ten days of pulse and water. Your line was keep it abroad. Where did you keep your small thing? Today, his three friends face something hotter than a menu. Day eight hundred seventy.

The band is the signal. On the plain of Dura, King Nebuchadnezzar has set up a great image of gold, and called every official in the land to stand before it. A herald explains the rule: when you hear the cornet, flute, harp, sackbut, psaltery, dulcimer, and every kind of music, fall down and worship the golden image. Whoever doesn't goes into a burning fiery furnace. The music starts. The whole plain goes down. Three men don't go down: Shadrach, Meshach and Abed-nego, the friends from yesterday. Someone reports them. The king, in a rage, has them brought in and gives them one more chance.
screen: `A GOLDEN IMAGE ON THE PLAIN.` → `THE MUSIC IS THE SIGNAL.` → `THREE MEN DON'T BOW.`

segments.voice: Their answer turns on three small words. In the King James words: "If it be so, our God whom we serve is able to deliver us from the burning fiery furnace, and he will deliver us out of thine hand, O king. But if not, be it known unto thee, O king, that we will not serve thy gods, nor worship the golden image which thou hast set up." But if not. They don't bargain. They don't say, we'll stand because we know we'll be rescued. They say God is able, and even if no rescue comes, the answer is still no. The furnace is heated, the text says, seven times hotter than usual; the men who throw them in are killed by the heat. Then the king jumps up, astonished. He counts. "Lo, I see four men loose, walking in the midst of the fire, and they have no hurt." Four. And the fourth, he says, looks like a son of the gods. Later the king himself says their God sent his angel. They went in bound. Now they're walking loose. When they come out, the text lists what isn't there: not a hair singed, their coats unchanged, and not even the smell of fire on them. The story doesn't say the fire wasn't real. It says they weren't alone in it.
screen: then, large: `ABLE TO DELIVER US. BUT IF NOT.` · `FOUR MEN LOOSE IN THE FIRE.` · `THEY WENT IN BOUND. NOW THEY WALK LOOSE.` · then: `NOT EVEN THE SMELL OF FIRE.`

segments.voice: Today's practice is to stand firm once, and it starts with three small words: but if not. Settle, and let your breath slow. Bring to mind one thing you've decided is right and mean to keep doing: a promise you made, a line you hold at work, an apology you owe, a way of telling the truth. First say to yourself what you hope will come of it. Then say the other half: but if not. If it doesn't go well, if no one thanks you, would you still do it? Take away the happy ending and see what's left. If the answer is still yes, that's the ground you stand on. If you pray, you can ask in words from your tradition not to be alone in it. The bell holds the time.
If not. The three words the friends anchor their answer on: God is able, but if not, the answer is still no. Today's word.
Your line: not alone in the fire. Today, do the thing you chose without waiting to see how it ends, and notice who stands with you. Day eight hundred seventy.

original.note: Aramaic, the language of this chapter of Daniel: and if not, from Daniel 3:18.

trapdoor: what you thought: a miracle story where faith guarantees you won't get burned.
what it means: three men refuse to bow "but if not", even with no rescue promised, and in the fire there's a fourth.
what a scholar hears: the fourth is never named in the chapter. the king first says he looks like a son of the gods, then says God sent his angel.

871.title: Weighed in the balances (Daniel 5)
871.hook: the writing on the wall: weighed, and found wanting
871.howItsDone: Some Jews keep a practice called cheshbon ha-nefesh, an accounting of the soul, looking honestly at their day or their year, especially in the month of Elul before Rosh Hashanah, and some do it each night before sleep.

segments.voice: Yesterday, three men said but if not, and walked loose in the furnace, and the king counted four. Your line was not alone in the fire. What did you do without waiting to see how it ends? Today, a different king, and a different kind of fire. Day eight hundred seventy-one.

King Belshazzar has been tasting the wine at his great feast when he calls for the cups. Not just any cups: the gold and silver vessels taken out of the Temple in Jerusalem. He and his lords, his wives and his concubines drink wine from them, and praise gods of gold and silver, brass, iron, wood and stone. In the same hour, the fingers of a man's hand appear and write on the plaster of the palace wall, near the lampstand. The king watches the hand write. His face changes. In the King James words, "his knees smote one against another." Nobody in the room can read what it says.
screen: `HOLY CUPS AT A ROYAL PARTY.` → `A HAND WRITES ON THE WALL.` → `NOBODY CAN READ IT.`

segments.voice: The king's wise men fail. The queen remembers a man from the old king's days, Daniel, and he's brought in. Belshazzar offers him scarlet clothes, a gold chain, a high place in the kingdom. Daniel's first words: "Let thy gifts be to thyself." He'll read it, but not for pay. Then, before reading, he tells the king a story the king already knows: how his father Nebuchadnezzar grew proud and was brought low. And then the sentence that matters: "thou his son, O Belshazzar, hast not humbled thine heart, though thou knewest all this." Though you knew. The charge isn't ignorance. It's knowing better and lifting the holy cups anyway. Then Daniel reads the wall. "MENE, MENE, TEKEL, UPHARSIN." Mene: God has numbered your kingdom and finished it. And then: "TEKEL; Thou art weighed in the balances, and art found wanting." Peres: your kingdom is divided, and given to the Medes and Persians. Weighed. Not shouted at, not argued with: put on a scale, and the scale reads light. The text doesn't linger. "In that night was Belshazzar the king of the Chaldeans slain." It's a frightening chapter, and it leaves a plain question for an ordinary evening: if today were set on a scale, what would be in the pans?
screen: `LET THY GIFTS BE TO THYSELF.` · `THOU KNEWEST ALL THIS.` · `NUMBERED, WEIGHED, DIVIDED.` · then, large: `THOU ART WEIGHED IN THE BALANCES.` · then: `WHAT'S IN THE PANS TODAY?`

segments.voice: Today's practice is to weigh your day honestly. Sit, and let your breath slow. Picture an old balance scale, two pans hanging level. Go back over today so far, or yesterday if it's early. In one pan, put what you did well: a kindness, a job done right, a moment you held your temper. In the other, what was wanting: a sharp word, a thing left undone, a time you knew better. Don't argue with the scale, and don't punish yourself with it. Just look. Then choose one good thing to put in the first pan before tonight. If you pray, you can bring both pans before God in words from your tradition. The bell holds the time.
Tekel. The word on the wall that Daniel reads as weighed, and found wanting. Today's word.
Your line: weighed in the balance. Today, before you sleep, check the scale once more, and see whether the one good thing you chose made it into the pan. Day eight hundred seventy-one.

what a scholar hears: the wall says upharsin, but Daniel reads it as peres, and he takes each word as a verb: numbered, weighed, divided.

872.title: Windows toward Jerusalem (Daniel 6)
872.hook: Daniel keeps praying three times a day, windows open toward Jerusalem, lions or not
872.tomorrow: They that be wise shall shine (Daniel 12:3)
872.howItsDone: Jewish tradition sets three services a day, Shacharit in the morning, Minchah in the afternoon and Maariv in the evening, facing toward Jerusalem, and the Talmud (Berakhot 31a) learns from Daniel 6 that one should pray in a room with windows.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a hand wrote on a palace wall, and Daniel read it: tekel, weighed, and found wanting. Your line was weighed in the balance. What did you put in the pan? Day eight hundred seventy-two.

The trap is a law. Under a new king, Darius, Daniel rises so high that the other officials go looking for something to accuse him of, and find nothing. So they say, in the King James words: "We shall not find any occasion against this Daniel, except we find it against him concerning the law of his God." They go to the king with a flattering idea. For thirty days, let no one ask a petition of any god or any man except the king. Whoever does goes into the den of lions. The king signs it, under the law of the Medes and Persians, which can't be changed. The trap is set. Everyone knows what Daniel does every day.
screen: `NO FAULT BUT HIS FAITH.` → `A LAW FOR THIRTY DAYS.` → `SIGNED, AND IT CAN'T CHANGE.`

segments.voice: Here is what he does: "Now when Daniel knew that the writing was signed, he went into his house; and his windows being open in his chamber toward Jerusalem, he kneeled upon his knees three times a day, and prayed, and gave thanks before his God, as he did aforetime." Look at what he doesn't do. He doesn't close the windows. He doesn't switch to praying in secret for a month. He doesn't march into the square to make a point either. He goes home, to his own room, and does what he did yesterday. As he did aforetime. The courage in this story looks like a habit. And notice which way the windows face. Toward Jerusalem, a city far away. He can't see it. He faces it anyway. The officials catch him, the king, who doesn't want this, tries until sundown to save him and can't, and Daniel goes into the den. At dawn the king runs to the stone and calls. Daniel answers: "My God hath sent his angel, and hath shut the lions' mouths, that they have not hurt me." This chapter left marks on Jewish prayer. Jewish tradition sets prayer for morning, afternoon and evening, said facing toward Jerusalem, and the Talmud, in tractate Berakhot, learns from this very verse that a person should pray in a room with windows.
screen: `HE DOESN'T CLOSE THE WINDOWS.` · `AS HE DID AFORETIME.` · `FACING A CITY HE CAN'T SEE.` · then, large: `HIS WINDOWS BEING OPEN TOWARD JERUSALEM.` · then: `THE LIONS' MOUTHS SHUT.`

segments.voice: Today's practice is a window open, the way Daniel kept his. If there's a window near you, turn toward it, or open it a little. If there isn't, turn toward the light in the room. Daniel faced a city he couldn't see. Let the window stand for whatever you face toward each day: a place, a hope, a person, God. Breathe in the air from outside. If you pray, this is your time, in words from your tradition or in silence, the way Daniel did it in his own room. If you don't, simply sit facing out, and let the day come in. The bell holds the time.
Jerusalem. The city Daniel's open windows faced, three times a day, lions or not, as he did aforetime. Today's word.
Your line: as he did aforetime. Today, keep one daily habit exactly on time, even if the day pushes against it. Day eight hundred seventy-two.

what a scholar hears: Jewish prayer still carries it: three times a day, facing Jerusalem, and the Talmud's rule to pray in a room with windows.

873.title: They that be wise shall shine (Daniel 12:3)
873.hook: the wise "shall shine as the brightness of the firmament"
873.howItsDone: In chavruta, a traditional way of Jewish study in pairs, two partners read a text aloud and explain it to each other, so that teaching is part of learning.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Daniel kneeled three times a day with his windows open, as he did aforetime. Your line was as he did aforetime. Which habit did you keep on time? Today, the last chapter of Daniel. Day eight hundred seventy-three.

What does a book of furnaces and lions end on? Not on a court story. The later chapters of Daniel turn into visions: beasts rising from the sea, kings rising and falling, messengers who explain and still leave much unexplained. By the last chapter, the vision has reached its darkest point. In the King James words, "there shall be a time of trouble, such as never was since there was a nation even to that same time." And right there, in the trouble, the text stops to say who will be shining.
screen: `FROM COURT STORIES TO VISIONS.` → `A TIME OF TROUBLE.` → `THEN, WHO WILL SHINE.`

segments.voice: Here's the line: "And they that be wise shall shine as the brightness of the firmament; and they that turn many to righteousness as the stars for ever and ever." Two kinds of light. The firmament is the whole sky, the bright dome over everything. The stars are points of light, each one on its own in the dark. Who are the wise? The Hebrew word is maskilim. A chapter earlier, the same book describes them: "they that understand among the people shall instruct many." So in Daniel, the wise aren't the ones who keep wisdom to themselves. They're the ones who pass it on, and the ones who turn many to righteousness shine like stars. Some readers hear in maskilim both things at once: those who are wise, and those who make others wise. And then comes a surprise, near the very end. Daniel himself, who read the wall and the dreams of kings, says this about his own vision: "I heard, but I understood not." He asks how it will end, and he's told: "Go thy way, Daniel: for the words are closed up and sealed till the time of the end." The man who read the wall doesn't get every answer. He's still told to go his way. You don't need to understand everything to teach the one thing you do understand. A star doesn't light the whole sky. It just shines where it is.
screen: `THE SKY, AND THE STARS.` · `THE WISE ARE THE ONES WHO INSTRUCT.` · `I HEARD, BUT I UNDERSTOOD NOT.` · then, large: `THEY THAT BE WISE SHALL SHINE.` · then: `ONE STAR, WHERE IT IS.`

segments.voice: Today's practice is to teach someone one thing. Sit back and breathe. Look over what you've learned on this path lately: a word, a story, a line, a practice. Esther's question. Daniel's open windows. The writing on the wall. Pick one thing you understand well enough to say in a sentence or two. Now think of one person who might like to hear it: a child, a friend, a parent, a coworker. Say the sentence to yourself, plainly, the way you'd say it to them. You don't have to know everything. One star's worth is enough. The bell holds the time.
Maskilim. The wise in Daniel's last chapter: those who instruct many, who shine like the sky and the stars. Today's word.
Your line: shine as the firmament. Today, teach your one thing to your one person, in a sentence or two. Day eight hundred seventy-three.

874.title: The return (Ezra 1)
874.hook: Cyrus of Persia lets the exiles go home to rebuild
874.carry: the ones who go and the ones who send
874.howItsDone: Moving to the land of Israel is called aliyah, going up, the same picture of going up that Cyrus's decree uses, and Jews who move to Israel today are said to make aliyah.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the last chapter of Daniel: the maskilim, the wise, shine as the firmament, and those who turn many to righteousness, as the stars. Your line was shine as the firmament. What did you teach, and to whom? Day eight hundred seventy-four.

"Thus saith Cyrus king of Persia." A proclamation goes out through a whole empire, spoken aloud and put in writing. The God of heaven, says the king, has given him all the kingdoms of the earth, and charged him to build a house in Jerusalem, in Judah. Then the line that opens the way home. In the King James words: "Who is there among you of all his people? his God be with him, and let him go up to Jerusalem." After all the chapters of loss, the book of Ezra opens with a door.
screen: `A PROCLAMATION FROM CYRUS.` → `BUILD A HOUSE IN JERUSALEM.` → `LET HIM GO UP.`

segments.voice: The book opens by saying why it happened: it was "in the first year of Cyrus king of Persia, that the word of the LORD by the mouth of Jeremiah might be fulfilled," and "the LORD stirred up the spirit of Cyrus." A foreign king, and the text sees God moving through him anyway. Help, again, from an unexpected place. Now listen to the shape of the decree. It isn't an order. It's an invitation: let him go up. Not everyone does. The text says the ones who rose up to go were all those whose spirit God had stirred. Others stay, and the text doesn't scold them. The people of each place help instead: they strengthen the travelers with silver and gold, goods and animals, and freewill offerings for the house of God. A return needs both, the ones who go and the ones who send them. Then Cyrus does one more thing. He brings out the vessels of the house of the LORD that Nebuchadnezzar had carried off from Jerusalem, counts them out to a leader of Judah, and sends them home. A few days ago, in Daniel, a king drank wine from vessels like these. Now they're being packed for the road. The return doesn't begin with a wall or a Temple. It begins with going up, and carrying back what was taken.
screen: `GOD STIRRED UP A FOREIGN KING.` · `LET HIM GO UP: AN INVITATION.` · `THOSE AROUND THEM SENT GIFTS.` · then, large: `THE VESSELS GO HOME.` · then: `GOING UP, CARRYING BACK.`

segments.voice: Today's practice is to go back to one thing. Sit, and let your breathing find its own pace. Think of the vessels, packed for the road after years in a foreign treasury. Is there something of yours that got left somewhere along the way? A song your family sang. A recipe nobody makes anymore. A language you grew up hearing. A skill you set down. Don't scold yourself for the distance. The decree didn't. Just hold the thing in your mind, the way an exile might hold the name of a city. Then find the first step to carry it back, small enough to take today. If you pray, you can ask in words from your tradition for your spirit to be stirred. The bell holds the time.
The return. Cyrus's decree in Ezra 1: let him go up to Jerusalem, and build the house of the LORD. Today's word.
Your line: the ones who go and the ones who send. Today, take the first small step back toward the thing you found, even five minutes' worth. Day eight hundred seventy-four.

fork.reveal: the ones whose spirit was stirred went up, and the neighbors who stayed sent them off with gifts. both are part of the return.

original.note: Hebrew: and let him go up, from Cyrus's decree in Ezra 1:3.

trapdoor: what you thought: the return was a forced move back home.
what it means: a foreign king invites the exiles to go up and rebuild, and sends back the vessels taken from the Temple.
what a scholar hears: the text says God stirred Cyrus's spirit to fulfill Jeremiah's word, and stirred the spirits of those who went: one verb, a king and a people.

875.title: Weeping and shouting (Ezra 3:10–13)
875.hook: at the new foundation the old weep and others shout, and no one can tell the sounds apart
875.howItsDone: At a Jewish wedding, by tradition, a glass is broken at the end of the ceremony, which some explain as remembering the destruction of Jerusalem even at a moment of great joy.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Cyrus said let him go up, and the exiles started home with the Temple vessels packed for the road. Your line was the ones who go and the ones who send. What did you take one step back toward? Today, they lay a foundation, and the week ends. Day eight hundred seventy-five.

Two sounds rise from the same building site, and they're both loud. The builders have just laid the foundation of the new house of the LORD in Jerusalem. The priests stand in their robes with trumpets. The Levites, sons of Asaph, stand with cymbals. And they sing back and forth, praising and giving thanks, in the King James words, "because he is good, for his mercy endureth for ever toward Israel." The people answer with a great shout. It should be a simple, happy scene. It isn't simple.

segments.voice: Here's what the text says next: "But many of the priests and Levites and chief of the fathers, who were ancient men, that had seen the first house, when the foundation of this house was laid before their eyes, wept with a loud voice; and many shouted aloud for joy." The old men had seen the first Temple. They're standing at the beginning of the second, and they weep. The text doesn't say why. Maybe grief for what was lost. Maybe the memory of what used to stand there. Maybe relief, after so long. Maybe all of it at once. And many others shout for joy at a beginning. Notice who is weeping: not doubters on the edge of the crowd, but priests and Levites, the same groups the text set at the center of the song, along with the heads of families. Then the next line: "So that the people could not discern the noise of the shout of joy from the noise of the weeping of the people." The text refuses to separate them. It doesn't say the joy drowned out the tears, or that the old men should have cheered up. Both sounds rise together, and the noise, it says, was heard afar off. Anyone listening from a distance heard one sound, made of both.

Daniel's windows stayed open toward Jerusalem. The wise shine as the firmament. The ones who go, and the ones who send. And today, weeping and shouting at once. Now the practice: allow mixed feelings. Bring to mind one thing in your life that holds two sounds: a new job and an old one, a child growing up, a move, a loss that also made room. Let both sounds be there. You don't have to choose which one wins. If you pray, you can bring both to God in words from your tradition. The bell holds the time.
Weeping and shouting. At the foundation of the second house, the old weep and others shout for joy, and no one can tell the sounds apart. Today's word.
